- The bill has a demand charge this version does not price: $7.00/kW/month on the highest half-hourly demand in 16:00–21:00, reset monthly. A battery can lower a demand charge, so leaving it out may understate what a battery is worth.
- Every battery figure below covers energy only. It is PARTIAL and cannot decide the answer.
- Battery size assessed: 10 kWh of usable capacity.
- Solar, for comparison: INDICATIVE payback about 9 years. It is not weighed against the battery here, because the battery could not be assessed.

THE DECISION RULE
A battery is recommended now only if its payback falls within both the battery's warranty and the years the household expects to stay in its home.
- The battery's payback, energy only (PARTIAL): 65.0 years.
- Warranty: 10 years. FAILED: the payback is outside it by 55.0 years.
- Expected years in the home: 20 years. FAILED: the payback is outside it by 45.0 years.
- While a charge on the bill is unpriced, these limits cannot decide the answer.

HOW THE SAVING AND THE PAYBACK ARE WORKED OUT
annual saving = kWh moved × (value on release − cost to store ÷ efficiency) + demand saving
payback = (installed price − rebate) ÷ annual saving
- kWh the battery moves in a year: 2,104 kWh
- what the battery charged with in a year: 2,338 kWh, of which 0 kWh (0%) was solar surplus that would otherwise have been exported and 2,338 kWh (100%) was imported from the grid
- value on release, the average rate where the battery discharged: 22.00 c/kWh
- cost to store, the average cost of what it charged with (the import rate when charging from the grid, the feed-in tariff forgone when charging from solar): 14.00 c/kWh
- round-trip efficiency: 90%
- cost to store per kWh delivered, after losses (cost to store ÷ efficiency): 15.56 c/kWh
- margin on each kWh moved (value on release − cost per kWh delivered): 6.44 c/kWh
- demand saving: $0 (not calculated: the demand charge is not priced, so this is PARTIAL)
- annual saving: $136
- installed price: $11,390; rebate: $2,584; net outlay: $8,806

WHAT THE PAYBACK LEAVES OUT (not priced)
- backup power in an outage. THE HOUSEHOLD SAID THIS MATTERS TO IT. The payback counts bill savings only; keeping essentials running in a blackout is not valued.
- independence from retailer price rises. Prices are held at today's rates, so protection from future rises is not valued.
- evening peak relief. Discharging in the evening eases the network's peak; nothing in the household's number pays for that.
- battery wear. Wear decides which kWh are worth moving (2.0 c/kWh) but is not subtracted from the saving.
- outliving the warranty. The payback (65.0 years) runs past the 10-year warranty, so the battery may not last long enough to break even.
- a planned EV. The EV the household plans (when is not given) is not in these bills, so the figures leave its charging out. 'Adding an EV' among what would change the assessment says what it would do.
- demand charge. $7.00/kW/month on the highest half-hourly demand in 16:00–21:00, reset monthly. On the bill but not priced, so the saving and payback cover energy only.

THE HOUSEHOLD'S STATED PRIORITIES
- a lower bill: the answer turns on the bill saving, which this version cannot complete

HOW CERTAIN THIS IS
- The bill splits use into time-of-use windows, so how much falls in each window is billed, not estimated; only the shape within each window is modelled.
- The figures come from one representative year, carried forward at today's prices. A different year's use or prices would give different figures: they are not a forecast.
- PARTIAL: a charge on the bill is not priced (see RECOMMENDATION).

THE HOUSEHOLD ASKS
Why is the payback so long?

Answer the question briefly, answering only what was asked: at most four sentences and under 100 words.
reply: The payback of 65.0 years comes from a margin of 6.44 c/kWh on the 2,104 kWh the battery moves each year. It charges entirely from the grid at 14.00 c/kWh, which becomes 15.56 c/kWh after losses, against 22.00 c/kWh on release, giving an annual saving of $136 against a net outlay of $8,806. That payback is PARTIAL, covering energy only, because it leaves out the $7.00/kW/month demand charge, which a battery can lower, so it may understate the battery's worth. That is why the answer is "Cannot assess".
